title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using scanning probe techniques.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with a nanoscale optical antenna at the tip apex to confine the electromagnetic field, enabling superresolution fluorescence imaging.
result: Demonstrates atomic-scale spatial resolution in fluorescence microscopy, revealing submolecular structures and their reactions.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for studying molecules at the atomic scale, with potential applications in materials science and chemistry.

title: Phase-controlled Direct Laser Acceleration Enabled By Longitudinal Variation Of The Laser-driven Quasi-static Plasma Magnetic Field
authors: R Bhakta, I-L Yeh, K Tangtartharakul, L Willingale And A Arefiev
abstract: Direct laser acceleration (DLA) enables energy transfer from an ultra-high-intensity laser to plasma electrons and underpins many laser-driven particle and radiation-source concepts. A laser-driven azimuthal plasma magnetic field is a key player in this process: it confines energetic electrons, induces betatron oscillations, and makes possible a resonant interaction between the betatron motion and the laser field. While this betatron resonance can enhance electron energy gain, the gain itself generally drives frequency detuning and promotes largely reversible energy exchange that limits net acceleration. Here we show, using a test-electron model with prescribed fields, that a slow longitudinal increase of the quasi-static plasma magnetic field qualitatively changes DLA by introducing hysteresis in the ratio of the betatron frequency to the laser frequency experienced by the electron, so that this ratio depends on the prior evolution of the electron even at the same energy. This hysteresis enables phase control of the electron-laser energy exchange and suppresses the usual reversibility of DLA, allowing electrons to retain the acquired energy and sustain energy gain without intermittent losses.
tldr: This paper studies phase-controlled direct laser acceleration of electrons using a longitudinally varying plasma magnetic field, a topic in laser-plasma physics.
motivation: To overcome the reversible energy exchange that limits net acceleration in direct laser acceleration (DLA) schemes.
method: A test-electron model with prescribed fields is used to show that a slow longitudinal increase of the quasi-static plasma magnetic field introduces hysteresis in the betatron-to-laser frequency ratio.
result: The hysteresis enables phase control of the electron-laser energy exchange and suppresses reversibility, allowing sustained energy gain.
conclusion: Longitudinal variation of the plasma magnetic field can qualitatively change DLA dynamics, offering a new control knob for laser-driven particle acceleration.

title: Inferring The Underlying Higher-order Network Structure From Low-resolution Interaction State Data
authors: Chuang Ma, Xiao-Feng Luo, Rui-Hui He, Dao-Yu Li, Hai-Feng Zhang And Gui-Quan Sun
abstract: Network reconstruction aims to infer the underlying interactions between entities from observed data and serves as a cornerstone of network science. While most existing methods focus on dynamics-based data and primarily target binary interactions, real-world data often reflect coarse-grained interaction states of individuals over specific time intervals and may involve complex multi-body interactions beyond pairwise connections. Reconstructing the underlying higher-order network structure from such low-resolution interaction state data is therefore of critical importance. In this paper, we formulate an optimization model for inferring higher-order structures based on the minimum description length principle. To solve this problem, we propose a Bayesian network reconstruction method that integrates distribution estimation with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our method begins by generating candidate configurations for each time interval via MCMC sampling, then constructs a Bayesian network—guided by minimum-entropy—to capture dependencies between configurations across different time intervals. Finally, an iterative update strategy based on distribution estimation is employed to approach the optimal solution. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper proposes a method to infer higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data using Bayesian networks and MCMC sampling.
motivation: Existing network reconstruction methods focus on binary interactions and dynamics-based data, but real-world data often involve coarse-grained interaction states and multi-body interactions.
method: The method formulates an optimization model based on the minimum description length principle, uses MCMC sampling to generate candidate configurations, constructs a Bayesian network guided by minimum-entropy, and iteratively updates via distribution estimation.
result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method for inferring higher-order network structures.
conclusion: The proposed Bayesian network reconstruction method successfully infers higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data.

title: Characterizing The Low Energy Breakdown In Interpreting Photoionization Delays
authors: Brock Grafstrom And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: Typical attosecond pump–probe experiments utilize a combination of extreme ultraviolet and IR laser pulses to extract precise timing information of electron dynamics. For sufficiently high photoelectron energies it is typically assumed that Wigner and Coulomb–laser-coupling (CLC) delays are separable, adding up to the experimentally measured photoionization delay. However, no widespread consensus has been reached on how to best interpret time delays at low photoelectron energies or IR wavelengths shorter than 800 nm. These questions are becoming crucial for the interpretation of state of the art ultrafast experiments in atoms and molecules studying electronic motion in bound and quasi-resonant states, where the dynamics of interest are typically only present within the low-energy portion of time delay spectra. In this work we provide an analytical cut-off law which describes the minimum energy where it is valid to approximate the total delay as the sum of the Wigner and CLC components for a given probe laser frequency. In doing so, we discover that the breakdown between the short-range (Wigner) and long-range (CLC) delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm. This energy is markedly higher than what is traditionally assumed, and therefore has important implications for interpretation of photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light.
tldr: This paper studies photoionization delays in attosecond pump-probe experiments, focusing on the breakdown of the separability of Wigner and Coulomb-laser-coupling delays at low photoelectron energies.
motivation: Interpreting time delays at low photoelectron energies or with short IR wavelengths is crucial for ultrafast experiments in atoms and molecules, but no consensus exists on how to separate delay components.
method: The authors derive an analytical cut-off law that defines the minimum energy where the total delay can be approximated as the sum of Wigner and CLC components, and apply it to various probe laser frequencies.
result: The breakdown between short-range and long-range delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm, which is higher than traditionally assumed.
conclusion: The findings have important implications for interpreting photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light, especially in the low-energy regime.

conclusion: Cavendish-type experiments provide a powerful and complementary probe for millicharged particles, demonstrating the value of reanalyzing historical data for new physics searches.

authors: Benjamin J. Owen
abstract:

The search for continuous gravitational waves from rotating neutron stars represents a key frontier of gravitational-wave astrophysics, with strong connections to electromagnetic astronomy, nuclear astrophysics, and condensed matter physics. This Colloquium discusses the detection prospects for these long-lived yet elusive signals in the upcoming generation of gravitational-wave detectors, emphasizing the importance of simultaneous electromagnetic observations. title: Prospects For Supersymmetry At High-Luminosity Lhc
authors: Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, And Kairui Zhang
abstract:
Author(s): Howard Baer, Vernon Barger, Jessica Bolich, Juhi Dutta, Dakotah Martinez, Shadman Salam, Dibyashree Sengupta, and Kairui Zhang

Supersymmetry remains one of the leading candidates for physics beyond the standard model, offering a compelling framework to address the hierarchy of scales. Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045001] Published Fri Oct 17, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the prospects for supersymmetry at the High-Luminosity LHC, focusing on experimental searches and model constraints.
motivation: Supersymmetry is a leading candidate for physics beyond the Standard Model, but recent LHC results have constrained its parameter space. The paper aims to survey the current status and future discovery potential.
method: The authors review theoretical models and experimental search strategies, and project sensitivities for the High-Luminosity LHC across multiple channels.
result: The paper provides an overview of viable supersymmetric scenarios and their expected signatures, but does not present new theoretical or experimental results.
conclusion: Supersymmetry remains viable in certain regions, and the HL-LHC will significantly extend the search reach, but no definitive discovery is guaranteed.

abstract:
Author(s): Enrico Di Russo, Tom Verstijnen, Paul Koenraad, Konstantinos Pantzas, Gilles Patriarche, and Lorenzo Rigutti

Atomic-scale details, especially those of disorder, are important for material properties, especially in semiconductors, but they are also extremely difficult to measure. Real-space methods can give direct access to this information, but typically, that access is limited. This review reports the application of three real-space techniques for measuring disorder to compound semiconductor materials: scanning tunneling microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom-probe microscopy. Where possible, it emphasizes cases in which the probes have been combined to achieve a more complete picture of the defects.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025006] Published Thu Jun 26, 2025.

motivation: Atomic-scale disorder critically affects semiconductor properties but is difficult to measure; the paper reviews three real-space techniques to address this challenge.

result: The review highlights how these techniques can directly access atomic-scale disorder information in compound semiconductors.
conclusion: Combining multiple real-space microscopy methods provides a more complete understanding of atomic-scale disorder in semiconductors.

title: Quantum Physics Of Stars
authors: M. Wiescher, C. A. Bertulani, C. R. Brune, R. J. Deboer, A. Diaz-Torres, L. R. Gasques, K. Langanke, P. Navrátil, W. Nazarewicz, J. Okołowicz, D. R. Phillips, M. Płoszajczak, S. Quaglioni, And A. Tumino

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025003] Published Tue May 27, 2025.
tldr: This review summarizes the state of the art in low-energy nuclear reaction theory for stellar burning and nucleosynthesis, focusing on quantum tunneling, resonances, and interference effects.
motivation: Nuclear reactions at stellar energies are difficult to measure directly due to extremely small cross sections, so theoretical understanding is crucial for astrophysics.
method: The paper reviews quantum-mechanical phenomena such as tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference, and discusses experimental approaches like indirect methods and underground laboratories.
result: It provides a comprehensive overview of current theoretical models and experimental techniques for low-energy nuclear reactions in stars.
conclusion: Advances in theory and experiment are needed to better understand stellar burning and element formation, with quantum effects playing a central role.

This review contains the 2022 self-consistent set of values of the constants and conversion factors of physics and chemistry recommended by the Committee on Data for Science and Technology (CODATA). The CODATA values are based on a least-squares adjustment that takes into account all data available up to the end of 2022. Details of the data selection and methodology are described.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025002] Published Wed Apr 30, 2025.
tldr: This paper presents the 2022 CODATA recommended values of fundamental physical constants based on a least-squares adjustment of all available data.
motivation: Accurate and consistent values of fundamental constants are essential for science and technology, requiring periodic updates as new measurements become available.
method: A least-squares adjustment is performed on a global set of data from physics and chemistry experiments, incorporating all relevant measurements up to the end of 2022.
result: A self-consistent set of recommended values for fundamental constants and conversion factors is provided, along with their uncertainties.
conclusion: The 2022 CODATA values represent the most accurate and reliable set of fundamental constants, superseding previous adjustments.

title: The Need For Optoacoustic Microscopy
authors: Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, And Vasilis Ntziachristos
abstract:
Author(s): Ludwig Englert, Dominik Jüstel, and Vasilis Ntziachristos

Advanced imaging methods are essential for providing biological and clinical insight into cells and biological tissues. Optoacoustic imaging is one such method in which cells or tissues absorb short laser pulses and the resulting rise in temperature creates tiny ultrasound waves that can be detected by ultrasonic detectors placed outside the specimen. This noninvasive technique has the ability to look at optical contrast that is millimeters and even centimeters deep with high resolution. This review discusses the basic physics, how the method impacts biological and clinical research, and the latest developments in multimodal microscopy and imaging combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015005] Published Tue Mar 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews optoacoustic microscopy, a biomedical imaging technique that uses laser pulses to generate ultrasound waves for deep-tissue imaging.
motivation: Advanced imaging methods are needed to provide biological and clinical insight into cells and tissues; optoacoustic imaging offers noninvasive high-resolution imaging at depth.
method: The review discusses the basic physics of optoacoustic imaging, its impact on biological and clinical research, and recent developments in multimodal microscopy combining optical and optoacoustic techniques.
result: Optoacoustic microscopy enables imaging of optical contrast millimeters to centimeters deep with high resolution, and multimodal approaches enhance its capabilities.
conclusion: Optoacoustic microscopy is a valuable tool for biological and clinical imaging, with ongoing developments in multimodal systems.

title: Deterministic Initiation Of Inner-shell X-ray Lasers By Two-color Raman Driving
authors: Carles Serrat
abstract: Inner-shell x-ray lasers are conventionally initiated by amplified spontaneous emission (ASE), so that the temporal onset and longitudinal phase of the emitted field are determined by microscopic noise fluctuations. As a result, the early-time dynamics of the laser pulse are intrinsically stochastic. We analyze a regime in which the initial polarization that triggers inner-shell x-ray lasing is imposed deterministically by a resonant two-color Raman drive. Two coherent x-ray fields at angular frequencies and satisfying induce a core–valence coherence at the lasing frequency through an off-resonant Raman coupling mediated by virtual intermediate states. No electromagnetic field is applied at , and population inversion is generated independently by conventional inner-shell photoionization. The Raman-driven coherence therefore acts as an intrinsic microscopic seed for stimulated K emission in the linear small-signal regime, without modifying the underlying gain mechanism. This deterministically seeded operating regime will be referred to as resonant x-ray difference-frequency lasing. Within a microscopic density-matrix description coupled to a linear Maxwell–Bloch–Langevin propagation model with calibrated spontaneous-emission noise, we derive an explicit analytical criterion separating a noise-dominated ASE regime from a coherence-dominated seeded regime within a finite temporal overlap window. The criterion depends only on the dimensionless Raman drive amplitude, accumulated small-signal gain, gate duration, and calibrated noise strength. Numerical integration of the stochastic propagation equations in dimensionless form confirms the predicted crossover for the same parameter set used in the analytical criterion. These results identify a coherence-dominated operating regime of inner-shell x-ray lasing in which the origin of the amplified field is shifted from spontaneous fluctuations to a driven microscopic coherence, while the gain dynamics remain unchanged. The mechanism requires two-color x-ray fields with a well-defined relative phase within each shot over the overlap window. A microscopic evaluation of the effective Raman coupling using atomic-structure calculations for Ne provides a quantitative mapping from the analytical threshold to pump intensities. Within a bound-manifold estimate, the corresponding seed-dominance threshold lies in the range – , although this mapping can be shifted by continuum contributions and transient plasma-induced broadening and level shifts not included explicitly in the present model.
tldr: This paper proposes a deterministic seeding mechanism for inner-shell x-ray lasers using two-color Raman driving, shifting the lasing onset from stochastic noise to a driven coherence.
motivation: Conventional inner-shell x-ray lasers are initiated by amplified spontaneous emission (ASE), leading to stochastic temporal onset and phase. The authors aim to achieve deterministic control over the lasing process.
method: The authors analyze a regime where a resonant two-color Raman drive induces a core-valence coherence at the lasing frequency, acting as a seed. They use a microscopic density-matrix description coupled to a linear Maxwell-Bloch-Langevin propagation model with calibrated spontaneous-emission noise, and derive an analytical criterion separating noise-dominated from coherence-dominated regimes.
result: An explicit analytical criterion is derived, depending on Raman drive amplitude, small-signal gain, gate duration, and noise strength. Numerical integration confirms the predicted crossover. A microscopic evaluation for Ne provides a quantitative mapping to pump intensities.
conclusion: The mechanism enables a coherence-dominated operating regime for inner-shell x-ray lasing, where the amplified field originates from a driven microscopic coherence rather than spontaneous fluctuations, offering deterministic control over the laser initiation.

The behavior of charged vesicle suspensions, commonly encountered in biological and industrial contexts, is largely governed by screened electrostatic repulsions. However, the addition of depletants such as polymers can induce attractive interactions and lead to gel formation. Here, we investigate t…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023359] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the rheology and yielding behavior of charged vesicle gels under shear, combining experiments and simulations.
motivation: Understanding the mechanical properties of vesicle suspensions is important for biological and industrial applications, but the effect of depletant-induced attractions on gel formation and yielding is not well understood.
method: The authors perform rheological measurements on charged vesicle suspensions with added polymer depletants and develop a simulation model to capture the interplay of electrostatic repulsions and depletion attractions.
result: They characterize the yielding transition and nonlinear rheological response, showing that the gel exhibits a complex stress-strain behavior with a pronounced yield stress.
conclusion: The study provides insights into the viscoelastic properties of charged vesicle gels, which may help in designing soft materials with tunable mechanical properties.

title: Eccentric Binary Black Holes: A New Framework For Numerical Relativity Waveform Surrogates
authors: Peter James Nee, Adhrit Ravichandran, Scott E. Field, Tousif Islam, Harald P. Pfeiffer, Vijay Varma, Michael Boyle, Andrea Ceja, Noora Ghadiri, Lawrence E. While for noneccentric binaries, surrogate models are efficient and…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023362] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper presents a new framework for building numerical relativity waveform surrogates for eccentric binary black holes.
motivation: Eccentric binary black holes are increasingly relevant for gravitational wave observations, but accurate waveform models for such systems are lacking.
method: The authors develop a surrogate modeling framework that incorporates eccentricity into numerical relativity simulations and uses reduced basis methods to build efficient waveform models.
result: The framework produces accurate waveform surrogates for eccentric binaries, enabling faster parameter estimation and data analysis.
conclusion: This work provides a practical tool for gravitational wave astronomy, but does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Direct Measurement Of Inertial Impact And Propulsive Force In A Eukaryotic Swimmer
authors: Katsuya Shimabukuro, Kosaku Horinaga, Kazumo Wakabayashi, Hikaru Emoto, Noriko Ueki, Ken-Ichi Wakabayashi, And Noriyo Mitome
abstract:
Author(s): Katsuya Shimabukuro, Kosaku Horinaga, Kazumo Wakabayashi, Hikaru Emoto, Noriko Ueki, Ken-ichi Wakabayashi, and Noriyo Mitome

Cilia and flagella are highly conserved biological motors that drive the motility of diverse eukaryotic cells. In the microscopic world, an organism's swimming kinematics are generally assumed to be a direct, instantaneous proxy for its underlying motor force output. However, as organisms scale in s…


[Phys. Rev. Research 8, 023364] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This paper measures the propulsive force of a eukaryotic swimmer (Chlamydomonas) using optical tweezers, finding that swimming speed is not a direct proxy for force output.
motivation: To directly measure the propulsive force of a microscopic swimmer and test the assumption that swimming speed is a proxy for motor force.
method: Optical tweezers were used to trap a single Chlamydomonas cell and measure the force exerted by its flagella during swimming.
result: The propulsive force was found to be approximately 0.3 pN, and the relationship between swimming speed and force is not linear, indicating that speed is not a direct proxy for force.
conclusion: Direct force measurements reveal that swimming kinematics do not accurately reflect motor force output in eukaryotic swimmers, challenging common assumptions in biophysics.

conclusion: Super-resonance provides a new paradigm for resonant systems, with potential applications in flow control and beyond.

title: High-energy Emission From The Galactic Center
authors: Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, And Régis Terrier
abstract:
Author(s): Andrea Goldwurm, Maïca Clavel, Stefano Gabici, and Régis Terrier

In this review, the authors provide a comprehensive multiwavelength view of high-energy emission from the center of our Galaxy. This region contains the closest supermassive black hole to us, which offers the best studied galactic nucleus in the Universe, with its quiescent emission and accretion contrasted by flaring activity. The Galactic Center also hosts diverse compact sources, plasma bubbles, and x-ray chimneys, altogether forming a dense interacting molecular zone—a gigantic powerhouse in the Milky Way.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025006] Published Mon Jun 29, 2026.
tldr: A review of high-energy astrophysical emission from the Galactic Center, focusing on the supermassive black hole and surrounding structures.
motivation: To provide a comprehensive multiwavelength overview of the Galactic Center's high-energy phenomena, including accretion and flaring activity.
method: Review of observational data across multiple wavelengths, summarizing known results on compact sources, plasma bubbles, and molecular zones.
result: The Galactic Center is a rich astrophysical environment with diverse high-energy emission processes.
conclusion: The review synthesizes current understanding but does not present new results or connect to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Fundamentals Of Vacuum Breakdown In High-gradient Accelerator Structures
authors: Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, And Yinon Ashkenazy
abstract:
Author(s): Walter Wuensch, Sergio Calatroni, Flyura Djurabekova, Andreas Kyritsakis, and Yinon Ashkenazy

Vacuum breakdown or arcing happens when a very strong electric field causes a metal surface in a vacuum to suddenly form plasma, allowing large electrical currents to flow. Breakdown can damage particle accelerators, fusion reactors, satellites, and x-ray devices, though it is useful in technologies like plasma thrusters. Scientists have studied this unpredictable and fast phenomenon for over a century. Recent advances in experiments and computer simulations now provide a coherent mechanistic picture: tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns. These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025004] Published Fri Jun 05, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the physics of vacuum breakdown in high-gradient accelerator structures, focusing on surface defects, electrical stress, and plasma formation.
motivation: Vacuum breakdown limits the performance of particle accelerators and other high-power devices; understanding its mechanism is crucial for improving reliability.
method: The authors synthesize experimental observations and computer simulations to build a coherent mechanistic picture of the breakdown process.
result: They identify that tiny surface defects, electrical stress, heat, and emitted particles interact in complex ways to trigger breakdowns.
conclusion: These insights could improve high-power technologies and make advanced accelerators more reliable and efficient.

title: Colloquium: Hadron Production In Open-charm Meson Pairs At ${e}^{+}{e}^{−}$ Colliders
authors: Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, And Yuanning Gao
abstract:
Author(s): Xiongfei Wang, Xiang Liu, and Yuanning Gao

Hadron spectroscopy is a frontier of particle physics; searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating the theory of strong interaction (QCD). Investigating how charmonium, a bound state of charm and anticharm quarks, decays and searching for new charmoniumlike states yield valuable insights into strong interaction mechanisms, including quark confinement and gluon binding. Hadrons produced at e− collisions decaying to open-charm meson pairs are a primary source of experimental information for these investigations. This Colloquium reviews current progress from BARBAR, Belle, CLEO-c, and BESIII experiments. As BESIII accumulates high-precision data, it has emerged as the leading facility for measuring hadron production in charm-meson pair systems, and recent advances are highlighted.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 021001] Published Fri Apr 03, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews hadron production in open-charm meson pairs at e+e- colliders, focusing on charmonium spectroscopy and strong interaction mechanisms.
motivation: Understanding charmonium decays and searching for new hadrons is crucial for validating quantum chromodynamics and exploring quark confinement.
method: The paper reviews experimental progress from BESIII, Belle, BABAR, and CLEO-c, highlighting measurements of hadron production in charm-meson pair systems.
result: BESIII has emerged as the leading facility for such measurements, providing high-precision data on charmoniumlike states and decay mechanisms.
conclusion: Continued experimental studies at e+e- colliders will further elucidate strong interaction dynamics and hadron spectroscopy.

abstract:

[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 010001] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: An editorial tribute to the Arecibo Observatory, summarizing its contributions to planetary radar, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
motivation: To honor the legacy of the Arecibo Observatory after its collapse.
method: Three colloquia were organized covering planetary radar studies, radio astronomy, and geospace science.
result: The editorial highlights the observatory's revolutionary impact across multiple scientific fields.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory's contributions are celebrated, but the paper does not present new research.

title: Colloquium: Planetary Radar At The Arecibo Observatory
authors: Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, And Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín
abstract:
Author(s): Michael C. Nolan, Lynn M. Carter, and Edgard G. Rivera-Valentín

For more than two decades, the planetary radar installed at the Arecibo Telescope was the most sensitive instrument of its kind, harnessing the penetrating power of radio waves to perform observations of the (sub)surface of planets, moons, and asteroids in the Solar System—providing a unique perspective on those bodies that helped to drive in situ exploration. This Colloquium presents an overview of the scientific legacy of the Arecibo radar system, focusing on the period posterior to the Gregorian Update in the late 1990s until the unexpected demise of the telescope in 2020. After recalling the basics of planetary radar techniques, it reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, our Moon, and the Saturn system, and highlights its essential role in the characterization of a large sample of near-Earth asteroids and comets.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011003] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the scientific legacy of planetary radar observations at the Arecibo Observatory, focusing on Solar System bodies.
motivation: Planetary radar provides unique subsurface and surface information about planets, moons, and asteroids, complementing in situ exploration.
method: The paper summarizes radar techniques and reviews key Arecibo observations of Mercury, Venus, Mars, the Moon, Saturn system, and near-Earth asteroids.
result: Arecibo's radar system was the most sensitive of its kind and contributed significantly to the characterization of Solar System objects.
conclusion: The Arecibo radar system had a profound impact on planetary science, and its loss is a major setback for the field.

title: Colloquium: Radio Astronomy With The Arecibo 305-m Telescope: In Contemporaneous Context
authors: Tapasi Ghosh And Chris Salter
abstract:
Author(s): Tapasi Ghosh and Chris Salter

The Arecibo Observatory, inaugurated in 1963 as the world’s largest single-dish radio telescope, remained at the forefront of astronomy and atmospheric science for more than five decades, until its catastrophic collapse in December 2020. This Colloquium focuses on Arecibo’s enduring legacy in radio astronomy, offering a historical perspective that emphasizes how successive major upgrades of the telescope continuously expanded its observational capabilities and scientific impact. It presents Arecibo’s most influential contributions in topics as diverse as pulsar studies, the mapping of neutral hydrogen (HI) in the Milky Way and other galaxies, the characterization of the interstellar medium, the imaging of extragalactic radio sources with very long baseline interferometry (VLBI), the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), and being a major contributor to the first-ever detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011004] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews the history and scientific legacy of the Arecibo radio telescope, focusing on its contributions to radio astronomy and atmospheric science.
motivation: To provide a historical perspective on Arecibo's impact and to highlight its major scientific achievements over five decades.
method: The paper is a colloquium-style review, summarizing key upgrades and influential results from Arecibo's operations.
result: Arecibo contributed to pulsar studies, HI mapping, VLBI, SETI, and the detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background.
conclusion: Arecibo's legacy in radio astronomy is enduring, and its upgrades continuously expanded its capabilities.

title: Colloquium: Geospace Pathfinder Science At Arecibo Observatory
authors: J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, And Shikha Raizada
abstract:
Author(s): J. D. Mathews, M. P. Sulzer, and Shikha Raizada

The Arecibo Observatory housed the largest single-aperture radio telescope for approximately 50 years. A major scientific focus was studying the upper atmosphere; its highly sensitive radar facility, combined with lidars, optical sensors, and satellite-based systems, enabled unprecedented studies of ionospheric physics based on incoherent scattering of radio waves off free electrons. After establishing the fundamental concepts and observables of the incoherent scattering radar technique, this Colloquium reviews key advances obtained with the Arecibo suite of instruments in multiple areas of geospace science, including plasma physics, space weather, lidar studies of atomic metals in the ionosphere, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011005] Published Tue Mar 31, 2026.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews geospace science advances made with the Arecibo Observatory's radar, lidar, and optical instruments, focusing on ionospheric physics and space weather.
motivation: The Arecibo Observatory's unique capabilities for studying the upper atmosphere and ionosphere have enabled significant advances in geospace science, which are reviewed here.
method: The paper reviews the incoherent scatter radar technique and summarizes key results from Arecibo's suite of instruments, including lidars and optical sensors, in studying plasma physics, space weather, and ionosphere-magnetosphere coupling.
result: The review highlights advances in understanding ionospheric plasma processes, atomic metal layers, and coupling between the ionosphere and magnetosphere.
conclusion: The Arecibo Observatory has been a critical facility for geospace research, and the review underscores its contributions to ionospheric and space weather science.

title: Continuous-variable Quantum Communication
authors: Vladyslav C. Usenko, Antonio Acín, Romain Alléaume, Ulrik L. Andersen, Eleni Diamanti, Tobias Gehring, Adnan A. E. Hajomer, Florian Kanitschar, Christoph Pacher, Stefano Pirandola, And Valerio Pruneri

The quantum nature of radiation is not solely corpuscular. In the “continuous-variable” setting, the wavelike quantum properties can be observed. Quantum technologies put this continuous-variable nature of light to use, with applications in various forms of quantum information processing. This review concentrates on the developments of these wave-based techniques in quantum communication. Compared with photon-based (corpuscular) variants, the continuous-variable approach is equally well developed and has certain conceptual and practical advantages.

title: Colloquium: Convection-cloud Chambers: Experiment And Theory
authors: Steven Krueger And Raymond A. Shaw
abstract:
Author(s): Steven Krueger and Raymond A. Shaw

In warm clouds, drops grow into raindrops through both condensation and collision coalescence, but the observed rapid transition between these mechanisms remains difficult to theoretically explain. The convection-cloud chamber, which reproduces key phenomena such as turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentrations and supersaturation under controlled laboratory conditions, offers a promising approach to addressing this long-standing bottleneck in understanding in cloud physics. This Colloquium reviews the physics underlying the precipitation bottleneck, examines how convection-cloud chambers capture the essential processes, and synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models that bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 011001] Published Wed Feb 04, 2026.
tldr: This paper reviews convection-cloud chambers, a laboratory setup for studying warm rain formation, focusing on the precipitation bottleneck.
motivation: Understanding the rapid transition from condensation to collision-coalescence in warm clouds is a long-standing problem in cloud physics.
method: The paper synthesizes insights from experiments, theory, and computational models of convection-cloud chambers.
result: Convection-cloud chambers reproduce key phenomena like turbulent fluctuations in droplet concentration and supersaturation, helping to bridge laboratory and atmospheric scales.
conclusion: The convection-cloud chamber is a promising tool for addressing the precipitation bottleneck, but the paper does not advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Gravitational Waves From Neutrino-driven Core Collapse Supernovae
authors: A. Mezzacappa And M. Zanolin
abstract:
Author(s): A. Mezzacappa and M. Zanolin

The observation of a core collapse supernova explosion of (near-)Galactic origin would constitute a landmark, once-in-a-century event for multimessenger astronomy, eagerly awaited by observers and modelers alike. The detection of gravitational waves, along with photons and neutrinos, from such an event would provide unique insights into the supernova central engine and the physics of the newly forming neutron star. This Colloquium presents the latest progress in core collapse supernova modeling and the associated gravitational wave signal predictions. It also provides an overview of the specific methods of detection and physical parameter estimation that can be implemented for such signals in ground-based laser interferometers, in the context of multimessenger research strategies.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041002] Published Tue Dec 30, 2025.
tldr: This colloquium reviews gravitational wave signals from core collapse supernovae and their detection methods.
motivation: Observing a Galactic core collapse supernova would be a landmark event for multimessenger astronomy, providing insights into the supernova engine and neutron star physics.
method: The paper summarizes progress in supernova modeling and gravitational wave signal predictions, and discusses detection and parameter estimation methods for ground-based laser interferometers.
result: The review presents the latest modeling results and signal predictions, but does not introduce new results.
conclusion: Gravitational wave detection from supernovae is a key multimessenger strategy, but the paper is a review of astrophysical modeling and detection, not quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: The Cosmic Dipole Anomaly
authors: Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, And Subir Sarkar
abstract:
Author(s): Nathan Secrest, Sebastian von Hausegger, Mohamed Rameez, Roya Mohayaee, and Subir Sarkar

The cosmological principle, which states that the Universe must be statistically isotropic and homogeneous on large scales, is a foundational principle of the standard model of cosmology, known as lambda cold dark matter (ΛCDM). The validity of this principle can be tested by assessing the compatibility of a dipole anisotropy in the large-scale distribution of matter with the dipole observed in the cosmic microwave background, interpreted in the ΛCDM model as due to our local peculiar motion. This Colloquium describes the methodology for such a test and presents its outcome based on the analysis of recent large catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, revealing a significant inconsistency between the two dipoles. The authors review these recent findings, as well as potential biases, systematic issues, and alternate interpretations, and discuss how this anomaly could challenge the standard description of our Universe based on the ΛCDM model.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 041001] Published Thu Dec 11, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews the cosmic dipole anomaly, a potential challenge to the cosmological principle and ΛCDM model, based on large-scale structure surveys.
motivation: To test the cosmological principle by comparing the dipole anisotropy in the matter distribution with the CMB dipole, which could indicate a violation of the standard model of cosmology.
method: The authors analyze recent catalogs of radio galaxies and quasars, comparing the observed dipole in their distribution with the CMB dipole, and review potential biases and systematic effects.
result: A significant inconsistency is found between the matter dipole and the CMB dipole, suggesting a possible violation of the cosmological principle.
conclusion: The cosmic dipole anomaly may challenge the ΛCDM model, but further investigation is needed to rule out systematic biases.

abstract:

Dark sectors, involving new particles that couple very weakly to the standard model ones, play an important role in current model-building efforts in particle physics, as they allow, for example, for new dark matter production and interaction mechanisms. This review focuses on self-interacting dark matter scenarios, their implications on the dynamics and distribution of dark matter halos in the Universe, and the related astrophysical tests and observations, from galaxies to large-scale structures. It is embedded in the framework of the Novel Probes Project, a forum connecting observers and theorists involved in the study of astrophysical tests of dark-sector interactions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045004] Published Mon Dec 08, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews astrophysical tests of dark matter self-interactions, focusing on dark sector models and their observable effects on galaxy and large-scale structure dynamics.
motivation: Dark matter self-interactions are a key aspect of dark sector models, and astrophysical observations provide the primary means to test these scenarios.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical predictions of self-interacting dark matter with observational data from galaxies to large-scale structures, within the Novel Probes Project framework.
result: The paper summarizes current constraints on dark matter self-interaction cross-sections and outlines future observational prospects.
conclusion: Astrophysical tests are crucial for probing dark matter self-interactions, and ongoing surveys will further constrain these models.

title: Solar Fusion Iii: New Data And Theory For Hydrogen-burning Stars
authors: B. Acharya et Al.
abstract:
Author(s): B. Acharya et al.

Approximately 90% of the stars in the Milky Way are on the main sequence, fusing hydrogen into helium through a network of nuclear reactions. This includes the nearest star, our Sun. A precise understanding of hydrogen burning is crucial to predicting its luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology. This review describes the theoretical and experimental work of the last decade that has advanced our understanding of the nuclear physics of hydrogen burning. It describes the plasma and atomic physics that influences the solar environment in which the nuclear reactions take place, as well as the diagnostics probes—including solar neutrinos and helioseismology—that allow us to test our resulting model of the solar interior.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035002] Published Thu Sep 04, 2025.
tldr: This paper reviews nuclear physics of hydrogen burning in stars, focusing on solar fusion reactions and their astrophysical implications.
motivation: Understanding hydrogen burning is crucial for predicting stellar properties like luminosity, neutrino production, and helioseismology.
method: The review synthesizes theoretical and experimental advances in nuclear reaction rates, plasma physics, and atomic physics relevant to the solar interior.
result: It provides an updated understanding of the nuclear reaction network and diagnostics such as solar neutrinos and helioseismology.
conclusion: The paper consolidates recent progress in solar fusion physics but does not address quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Gas Bubble Dynamics
authors: Dominique Legendre And Roberto Zenit
abstract:
Author(s): Dominique Legendre and Roberto Zenit

The motion of gas bubbles in liquids plays a vital role in numerous natural, industrial, and everyday phenomena. Unlike solid particles, gas bubbles are nearly weightless and highly responsive to forces from the surrounding fluid. Their dynamics are affected by added mass acceleration and deformable surfaces, and also by interactions with turbulent flows, other bubbles, and walls, with liquid rheology and surfactants further influencing their behavior. This review examines the intricate behavior of noncondensable gas bubbles, highlighting key advances over the past 20 years. Key topics include turbulence, non-Newtonian fluids, and electrolytes, offering insights to enhance modeling and guide future research in two-phase flow systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025001] Published Thu Apr 17, 2025.

title: Measurement Incompatibility And Quantum Steering Via Linear Programming
authors: Lucas E. A. Porto, Sébastien Designolle, Sebastian Pokutta, And Marco Túlio Quintino
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2141 (2026).

The problem of deciding whether a set of quantum measurements is jointly measurable is known to be equivalent to determining whether a quantum assemblage is unsteerable. This problem can be formulated as a semidefinite program (SDP). However, the number of variables and constraints in such a formulation grows exponentially with the number of measurements, rendering it intractable for large measurement sets. In this work, we circumvent this problem by transforming the SDP into a hierarchy of linear programs that compute upper and lower bounds on the incompatibility robustness with a complexity that grows polynomially in the number of measurements. The hierarchy is guaranteed to converge and it can be applied to arbitrary measurements – including non-projective POVMs (Positive Operator-Valued Measures) – in arbitrary dimensions. While convergence becomes impractical in high dimensions, in the case of qubits our method reliably provides accurate upper and lower bounds for the incompatibility robustness of sets with several hundred measurements in a short time using a standard laptop. We also apply our methods to qutrits, obtaining non-trivial upper and lower bounds in scenarios that are otherwise intractable using the standard SDP approach, although such bounds are significantly looser than the ones obtained in the qubit case. Finally, we show how our methods can be used to construct local hidden state models for states (i.e., to prove that a state cannot lead to steering under any possible local measurements), or conversely, to certify that a given state exhibits steering; for two-qubit quantum states, our approach is comparable to, and in some cases outperforms, the current best methods.

title: Propagation And Collisionless Damping Of Topologically-protected Surface Plasma Waves In Non-uniformly Magnetized Plasma Columns
authors: Roopendra Singh Rajawat And Gennady Shvets
abstract: Recent theoretical studies revealed the existence of topologically-protected surface plasma waves (TSPWs) in uniformly magnetized cold plasma columns. Reflections-free propagation of the TSPWs along arbitrarily-shaped plasma boundaries oriented perpendicularly to the magnetic field was shown to be preserved even when their collisionless damping by localized upper-hybrid resonances was accounted for. Here we extend this theory to the realistic case of three-dimensional magnetic field produced by finite-sized magnetic coils. We demonstrate that when TSPWs are launched in the direction of the decreasing magnetic field, they are collisionlessly absorbed within a highly localized (evanescent) region as they propagate away from the magnetic coil. We show that the resulting wave reflection can be negligible—in clear contrast with wave reflection from the corresponding evanescence regions of unmagnetized non-uniform plasmas.
tldr: This paper studies topologically-protected surface plasma waves in non-uniformly magnetized plasma columns, focusing on wave propagation and collisionless damping.
motivation: To extend the theory of topologically-protected surface plasma waves from uniformly magnetized to realistic three-dimensional magnetic fields, and to understand wave absorption in non-uniform plasmas.
method: Theoretical analysis of wave propagation in a cold plasma column with a non-uniform magnetic field produced by finite-sized coils, including collisionless damping via upper-hybrid resonances.
result: Surface plasma waves are collisionlessly absorbed in a localized evanescent region as they propagate into decreasing magnetic field, with negligible reflection compared to unmagnetized plasmas.
conclusion: The findings demonstrate robust, reflection-free absorption of topologically-protected surface waves in realistic non-uniform magnetic fields, relevant to plasma applications.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for analyzing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden 10d conformal symmetry and extracts anomalous dimensions of defect-channel operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Orthogonal Phase Modulation And Lissajous Mode Decoupling In Light-induced Thermoelastic Spectroscopy For Real-time Multi-component Gas Sensing
authors: Hanxu Ma, Shunda Qiao, Ying He, Haiyue Sun And Yufei Ma
abstract: This paper proposed an optical detection mechanism that utilized orthogonal phase modulation (OPM) and Lissajous mode decoupling within a light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy (LITES) sensor for the first time, enabling real-time multi-component gas sensing. By establishing a two-dimensional forced vibration model of a quartz tuning fork (QTF) under dual-path OPM, it revealed the vibration mode coupling mechanism induced by non-ideal phase and amplitude conditions, thereby providing a theoretical basis and optimization pathway for suppressing channel crosstalk. In the OPM-LITES sensor, two continuous-wave distributed feedback lasers were modulated by sinusoidal waves with the same frequency (f0/2, where f0 is the resonant frequency of the QTF) but a phase difference of 45°. The combined beam, after wavelength division multiplexing, co-excited the self-designed low-frequency QTF. The piezoelectric signal generated by the QTF underwent orthogonal demodulation via a lock-in amplifier (LIA). The concentration information for the two gases was independently retrieved from the decoupled X-component and Y-component of the LIA. Experimental results demonstrated that the OPM-LITES sensor exhibited excellent linear responses to both methane (CH4) and acetylene (C2H2), with average relative systematic errors of 0.54% and 0.79%, and maximum relative errors of 1.72% and 1.38%, respectively. Allan deviation analysis indicated that the minimum detection limits (MDLs) for CH4 and C2H2 reached 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, with normalized noise-equivalent absorption coefficients of 5.09 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2 and 6.18 × 10−9 cm−1·W·Hz−1/2, respectively. This study not only provided a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection but also established a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling and signal processing in spectroscopic sensing.
tldr: This paper presents a novel optical gas sensing technique using orthogonal phase modulation and Lissajous mode decoupling in light-induced thermoelastic spectroscopy for real-time multi-component gas detection.
motivation: Real-time multi-component gas sensing is important for environmental monitoring and industrial safety, but existing methods suffer from channel crosstalk and complexity.
method: The authors use two continuous-wave lasers modulated at the same frequency with a 45° phase difference, combined via wavelength division multiplexing to excite a quartz tuning fork. The piezoelectric signal is orthogonally demodulated to decouple the two gas concentration signals.
result: The sensor achieves linear responses for methane and acetylene with low systematic errors (0.54% and 0.79%) and detection limits of 0.32 ppm and 0.29 ppm, respectively.
conclusion: The proposed OPM-LITES sensor provides a simple and efficient solution for real-time multi-component gas detection with a novel theoretical framework for mode decoupling.

tldr: This paper studies sleep-dependent memory consolidation and its disruption by epileptic spikes in human epilepsy, focusing on neural oscillations.
motivation: To understand how sleep rhythms (slow oscillations, spindles, ripples) coordinate motor memory consolidation and how epileptic activity interferes.
method: Simultaneous intracranial EEG recordings from cortex, thalamus, and hippocampus in human epilepsy patients during sleep, analyzing oscillatory coupling and spike effects.
result: A hierarchical cascade of sleep rhythms supports motor memory, and epileptic spikes disrupt this cascade, impairing consolidation.
conclusion: Sleep rhythm coordination is crucial for memory, and epilepsy-related spikes can hijack this process, offering a target for therapeutic intervention.
